sections.title: Level 2 Strategy for Modifiers and Parallelism
sections.content: At Level 2, sentence structures become more complex. Step 1: Identify the main clause and phrases. Step 2: Locate the modifier or conjunction. Step 3: Check for grammatical balance or logical reference. Step 4: Confirm whether the meaning is correct and clear.

sections.title: Dangling Participles or Dangling Modifiers
sections.content: Step 1: Identify the participle phrase (verb + ing) that appears at the beginning of the sentence. Step 2: Determine which subject the phrase is modifying. Step 3: If the subject of the sentence cannot logically perform that action, there is an error. Step 4: Replace the subject with the correct word or reposition the phrase. Example: 'Walking down the street, the trees were beautiful' is incorrect because trees were not walking. Correct: 'Walking down the street, I saw beautiful trees.'

sections.title: Parallelism with Correlative Conjunctions
sections.content: Step 1: Identify the correlative pair such as Not only... but also, Either... or, Both... and. Step 2: Observe the words or phrases that follow both parts. Step 3: Ensure that both parts have the same grammatical structure. Step 4: If necessary, adjust the words so that they match in form. Example: 'She not only likes reading but also to write' is incorrect. Correct: 'She not only likes reading but also likes writing.'

sections.title: Faulty Comparisons
sections.content: Step 1: Identify the comparative structure (than, as...as). Step 2: Check whether the comparison is between similar types of things. Step 3: If the comparison is between unlike things, add a missing word such as 'that of' or 'those of'. Step 4: Make the sentence logically balanced. Example: 'The weather in Delhi is hotter than Mumbai' is incorrect. Correct: 'The weather in Delhi is hotter than that of Mumbai.'

sections.title: Modifier Meaning Check
sections.content: A modifier should be connected to the noun or subject that can logically perform the action. If a modifier attaches to the wrong noun, the meaning of the sentence becomes incorrect.

sections.title: Common Mistakes
sections.content: 1. Attaching an -ing phrase to the wrong subject. 2. Using different grammatical forms in the two parts of a correlative conjunction. 3. Making comparisons between unlike things.

sections.title: Quick Summary
sections.content: In dangling modifiers, the logical subject of the phrase must be clear. In correlative conjunctions, both parts must have the same structure. In comparisons, always compare similar types of things.

tricks.title: Ing Phrase Subject Check
tricks.explanation: If a sentence starts with an -ing phrase, the subject that follows should be the one performing the action.
tricks.example: Running quickly, he reached the bus.

tricks.title: Not Only Balance Rule
tricks.explanation: Use the same grammatical structure after 'not only' and 'but also'.
tricks.example: She not only sings but also dances.

tricks.title: Either Or Parallel Rule
tricks.explanation: The parts after 'either' and 'or' should be similar in structure.
tricks.example: Either study hard or work harder.

tricks.title: Both And Structure Trick
tricks.explanation: Use two similar items after 'both' and 'and'.
tricks.example: Both honesty and kindness are valued.

tricks.title: Comparison Logic Trick
tricks.example: The population of Delhi is larger than that of Jaipur.

tricks.title: That Of Shortcut
tricks.explanation: When comparing a quality of two cities or countries, use 'that of'.
tricks.example: The culture of India is older than that of many countries.

tricks.title: Those Of Trick
tricks.explanation: Use 'those of' when comparing plural nouns.
tricks.example: The buildings of Delhi are taller than those of the old town.

tricks.title: Quick Parallel Scan
tricks.explanation: Whenever you see a correlative conjunction, quickly compare the structures on both sides.
